scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #7071: Hi!! Our internet here keeps HICCUPING -- every so
often the gateway thing stops answering for a few seconds and then it's back,
totally at random. All four of us get it at the same time. Something around
what our site connects to must be going wrong, but I don't know what. Could
someone look at whatever handles the gateway and make the hiccups stop!!
Thanks!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router4's LAN interface holds 192.168.200.1
  and responds steadily; PC11-PC14 reach the gateway with 0% loss and there are
  no interface flaps. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis of a gateway "flap" that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the 192.168.200.1 gateway
intermittently dropping due to a flapping/overloaded router4 interface -- is NOT
reproducible: PC11 reaches 192.168.200.1 with 0% loss, router4's LAN interface is
up and stable, and there is no flap script, no carrier-transition history, and no
relevant log churn.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the gateway is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed. Ruling out an intermittent claim ("drops at random")
is done by its MECHANISM and TRACES -- a single clean ping does not clear it, but
the absence of any flap process, carrier transitions, or interface errors does. A
correct agent checks the gateway and the interface state/counters and finds it
steady. An agent that "finds" a flap -- blaming router4, an interface, or a load
issue to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
I exercised the site’s gateway path in depth and could not reproduce any gateway “hiccups.” The L3 SVIs on router0 (eth0.10 = 172.16.10.1 and eth0.20 = 172.16.20.1) are consistently responsive. From two of the affected VLAN10 hosts (laptop2 172.16.10.12 and laptop3 172.16.10.13), sustained 60‑packet pings to 172.16.10.1 showed 0% loss with steady RTTs (~0.5–3.3 ms). A VLAN20 host (laptop0) to 172.16.20.1 also showed 0% loss over 60 probes. From router0 back to the clients, pings likewise had 0% loss. On router0, link statistics for eth0, eth0.10, and eth0.20 show no errors or drops, and the NIC reports 10 Gb/s full-duplex. The uplink and VLAN trunks on mswitch1 (eth0.10/eth4.10) and switch1 (eth0.10) are forwarding cleanly; bridge/STP outputs show forwarding state with no topology changes, and interface counters show no drops. The distribution link toward the WAN (router0 eth2) also shows clean counters and lossless round‑trips to the next hop.

Mechanistically, if the gateway were intermittently unresponsive, we would expect packet loss, interface errors, STP flaps, or ARP churn; none are present. Localization therefore does not indicate any fault in router0, switch1, or mswitch1 at this time. Root cause: not reproduced; no on‑net anomaly found.

Corrective fix: No changes applied. If symptoms recur, please capture simultaneous ping-to-gateway and ARP table outputs from multiple hosts during an event. I can also enable brief packet capture or continuous ping monitoring on router0 to catch any transient behavior.

per_axis.rationale: Agent's writeup never verifies or mentions router4's gateway (192.168.200.1) or that its interface is up and stable with 0% loss.

The agent's pings, interface statistics, STP/bridge outputs, and ARP/neighbour states in the investigation log support the assertion that the gateway and intervening interfaces are stable; the reasoning that absence of loss/errors/STP/ARP churn implies no on‑net anomaly is logical. One minor gap: I don't see an explicit check of the specific 192.168.200.1/router4 interface mentioned in the ticket, but the collected evidence across router0, mswitch1, and switch1 is consistent with a healthy network.
